articles.title: Turmoil within Dolly Parton’s estate underscores the precariousness of family businesses after founders die
articles.author: Reid Kress Weisbord, Distinguished Professor of Law, Rutgers University - Newark
paras: Dolly Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver announced the legendary singer’s death on Aug. 25, 2026, in a prerecorded video. Seaver, the son of one of Parton’s 11 siblings, had been her head of security for many years.
But Seaver is currently embroiled in a messy dispute with She’s Alive LLC, the company Parton established to manage her business assets after her death.
This unusually acrimonious fight highlights some of the business succession problems that can arise when the founder of a company dies but wants its other leaders to keep it going.
Parton, a legendary American singer, actress, entrepreneur and philanthropist, left behind an estimated US$450 million estate.

She’s Alive LLC terminated Seaver’s involvement with the business, and a court has issued a restraining order against him. Seaver is accused of engaging in “an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats” against Parton’s estate. He denies the allegations.

As professors who research and teach topics related to inheritance law, we are fascinated by the Parton case. It illustrates some of the pitfalls of planning for the transition of a privately held business after the founder’s death – a concern for celebrity and noncelebrity estates alike.
Managing celebrity estates after death

Celebrity estates, like Parton’s, are distinct because they often contain valuable intellectual property. This includes copyrights, which protect creative works, such as songs and recordings, including Parton’s catalog of hits. Another valuable asset in these estates are publicity rights, which protect the use of the celebrity’s name or likeness, such as the use of Parton’s face on a T-shirt sold for profit.

These rights can be enormously valuable long after the celebrity has died. Without careful planning beforehand and appropriate management after death, the estate may never get the full value of these property interests.

Prince, for example, died in 2016 without a will or any formal estate plan. The twice-divorced Minneapolis pop star had no surviving children. His estate passed to his siblings, who were his sole heirs.

It took more than six years to administer his complicated $156 million estate, which concluded with the heirs establishing corporate entities to manage his intellectual property rights. One of those entities, Prince Legacy LLC, recently became embroiled in litigation when some of Prince’s heirs sought to fire the managers who had been hired to manage their share of the intellectual property rights.

Marilyn Monroe, who died in 1962, also without any children, left behind a professionally drafted will under which her longtime acting coach, Lee Strasberg (and his then-wife) inherited most of her publicity rights. But Strasberg remarried, and his widow – a woman whom Monroe never met – hired various professional managers, including a company known as CMG Worldwide, which specializes in the management, marketing and promotion of publicity rights associated with dead celebrities.
Because of the successful management of her estate’s publicity rights, Monroe became known as one of the highest-paid dead celebrities – with large sums enriching a woman she’d never met.
Should a founder’s relatives remain in charge?
Many much-less famous family businesses face similar questions about how to keep their profits and revenue flowing and who should manage the company after the founder of a family business dies.

A continuation of business operations may have many benefits for a deceased founder’s family. The founder may have relayed their succession plans to them. Relatives often have institutional knowledge and loyalties that can enhance the value of the business and make it last longer.
Studies have not conclusively shown, however, whether continuing a business within the family is clearly better or worse for its bottom line than having outsiders manage it.

As one study found, family managers often have a “sense of kinship obligation” and enjoy “personal and social fulfillment” from working together in the business. That, in turn, creates incentives to manage the firm carefully with an eye toward long-term survival.
By contrast, another study of small and medium-size businesses after the sudden death of a CEO-owner found that, in the short run, nonfamily successors are better equipped to run the company.

Relatives, by contrast, may be hampered by grief and the emotional impact of the death. But the study also found that in the long run, family members may be more successful in managing the business because they “are likely to view the firm’s survival as a way to stay connected with the deceased family member and keep their memory alive. In turn, this is expected to inspire great stewardship towards the firm.”

Other studies, however, have found that maintaining family control over the management of a company after its founder’s death can hurt its performance. Restricting the pool of potential managers to relatives excludes better-qualified candidates who can bring expertise and experience that members of the family lack. Research has shown that hiring pros tends to be best for the business.
Death can be bad for business

When the owner of a privately held business dies, their assets, including real property, intellectual property and investments, will pass to others according to the estate plan, if the owner created one.
But in many cases, the true value of a business is more than just the sum of all its assets. Some of the value may reside in the owner’s talent, knowledge and business acumen.

In some cases, the owner maintained personal relationships with employees or customers that may have played a key operational role. In others, the owner may have relied upon unique personal qualities to achieve success in business. Parton herself, for example, was likely the most significant driver of value for her business because of her creativity and star power.
According to a 2022 study by economists who studied what happened to startups following the death of nearly 1,500 business founders, growth and profitability fell after the founder’s death.
Smaller companies are at risk of having to close altogether.

The study found that the negative effects on business continuity “appear to be driven by entrepreneur specialness rather than leadership transition,” which suggests that the founder’s unique contributions to the business can be difficult to replicate after death even with excellent transition planning.
What this means for Parton’s estate

Parton’s full estate plan is not yet publicly known, but she did not have any children, and her husband died before her. According to court filings, Parton engaged in “extensive estate planning measures” that included trusts and various corporate entities to manage her business assets and intellectual property rights.

She gave generously to charity, with acclaimed gifts for medical research and disaster relief. She also created the Imagination Library through her Dollywood Foundation. It sends free books to millions of children from their birth until their fifth birthday.

The amount that anyone – family, friends or charities – will receive from the estate of a wealthy celebrity depends on how their business assets and intellectual property rights are managed after death. Parton planned carefully, but it is up to others to make the most of what she left behind.

articles.title: Economics Nobel: how this year’s winners helped to smooth the cycle of economic peaks and troughs
articles.author: Conor O'Kane, Senior Lecturer in Economics, Bournemouth University
paras: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has awarded this year’s Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences to the American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford. The prize was awarded in recognition of their development of macroeconomic models that helped to reduce the length and depth of economic downturns.

According to the Academy, the economists’ work in macroeconomic modelling has given policymakers additional tools to smooth out the economic cycle. As well as reducing the severity of downturns, their work also helped to cool the potentially negative impacts of economic booms.

Economies are known to follow cycles of downturns and upturns – and economists have long sought to find ways to tame these. More than a century ago, British economist John Maynard Keynes developed an approach to managing the economy that came to be known as Keynesianism.

Before this, the classical “laissez-faire” approach dominated. According to this doctrine, in an economic downturn, markets would eventually clear and the economy would rebound. Any attempt by government to directly influence the economy would not work and could even make things worse.

Keynes disagreed with the classical view. He believed that economies could get locked into a downward spiral that would deepen recessions and lead to economic depression. Instead, he argued that governments could actively use the levers of monetary policy (adjusting interest rates) and fiscal policy (lowering taxes and government spending) to improve the health of the economy.

In the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street crash, the US was in a deep economic depression. Franklin D. Roosevelt won a landslide presidential victory in 1932 and his “New Deal” approach to economic policy was similar to what Keynes advocated. The US economy recovered, and the Keynesian school would dominate policymaking in many advanced economies after the second world war.

But the oil crisis of the 1970s changed everything. The Keynesian approach was ineffective in dealing with low growth, spiralling inflation and high unemployment. Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher won elections in the US and UK with promises of “smaller government” economic policy, including lower taxes, privatisation and deregulation. Keynesianism needed a rebuild.
Decisions of consumers and businesses

Hall and Woodford became part of the “New Keynesian” school that emerged in the 1980s. Their approach was to build models that looked at decisions made by millions of individuals and businesses rather than just considering macroeconomic variables like production, inflation, consumption and unemployment.

Hall, of Stanford University in California, is an expert in consumption theory. According to his “random walk hypothesis”, decisions made by households on whether to spend or save were directly influenced by their expectations about future income and economic conditions. In other words, they were not just based on their current financial conditions. As consumption makes up around 70% of GDP in advanced economies, these insights were important.

Woodford, of Columbia University in New York, is an expert in supply-side macroeconomics, specifically the role that expectations play in price-setting and inflation. In his 2003 book, Interest and Prices: Foundations of a Theory of Monetary Policy, he proved that a central bank could influence economic activity by managing the public’s expectations about what might happen to interest rates in future.

Up until the 1990s, central bank policymaking was secretive and could sometimes take markets by surprise. Hall and Woodford’s insights changed this. In the aftermath of the 2008 global financial crisis, the central banks of most major advanced economies adopted an approach known as “forward guidance”.

This policy saw central bank governors provide greater transparency about their monetary policy intentions. Forward guidance policy announcements provide a clear assessment of both the economic outlook and how this might affect inflation. They also set out how central bank policy could react to these assessments.

As with most policy approaches, forward guidance has both advocates and critics. Research from the European Central Bank shows that clear communication from central banks reduces short-term interest rate volatility. There is also some evidence that after the 2008 financial crisis, expectations that inflation would remain low helped to keep interest rates down. This probably encouraged spending and investment, which aided economic recovery.

But critics believe that forward guidance has no impact on long-term interest rates and say it is debatable if it has any impact on short-term rates. They also argue that setting expectations about interest rates can strip credibility from central banks. This could happen if economic policy needs to be altered to deal with sudden shocks, for example.

The conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine are driving up energy prices and inflation expectations. The forward guidance from many central bankers is pointing to higher inflation and perhaps the need for higher interest rates.

Anyone coming off a fixed-rate mortgage might be sceptical of the idea that policy tools can lower short-term interest rate expectations. This is not to say that Hall and Woodford’s work has not been transformative. But economies are difficult beasts – and debates around central bank policymaking are sure to continue.

articles.title: Unpicking the pensions triple lock: where it came from, and what might happen next
articles.author: Maria Evandrou, Professor of Gerontology, University of Southampton
paras: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has made the politically risky decision to adjust the pensions triple lock from April 2030.

Speaking at this year’s Labour Party Conference, he said: “Some may not realise it but older people with nothing more than the state pension, or only a little more, can find themselves paying care charges today from that small income. Under my plan, this will no longer happen.”
But what is the triple lock, and why was the announcement so controversial?

The triple lock is a mechanism that provides a guaranteed increase in the basic and new state pension. It raises it by whichever is highest among average earnings growth, price inflation, or 2.5% and ensures that state pension payments increase in value every April.

Politicians have long considered any challenge to the triple lock to be highly risky to their chances at the ballot box. But how long has the mechanism been in place and what were the reasons for its introduction?

Increasing the value of pensions has been hotly debated since the early 1970s. Back then, the Labour government introduced legislation to increase long-term benefits and state pensions in line with earnings or prices, whichever was higher – a “double lock” on pensions growth.

But by the late 1970s, the governing Conservative party deemed this mechanism “unsustainable” because of the same “ratchet effect” that the triple lock is now criticised for. In other words, for the rest of the population, their wages grew in response to inflation – but pensioners enjoyed the rise every year. Pensions were then linked to prices only, rather than slower-growing earnings.

During the 1980s and 1990s, concerns grew about a growing number of people falling into poverty in later life. Consecutive governments debated whether the link to earnings should be restored. At the same time, pensioners were experiencing a steady decrease in the value of the state pension relative to average earnings. This went from a peak of 26% of average earnings in 1979 to around 16% of average earnings between 2000 and 2010.

In 1999, there was a reckoning when pensioners received an increase of just 75p per week after a period of low inflation. The tiny uptick sparked anger and then-chancellor Gordon Brown was under pressure to act. Finally, in 2002, the Labour government legislated to increase pensions by the higher of 2.5% or price inflation. The double lock was back in place.

A key point came when the (first) Pensions Commission in 2005 published its recommendation that the government restore the link of pensions with earnings. This was a bid to reduce the risk of pensioners falling into poverty and placing pressure on the system of means-tested benefits.

This recommendation was followed by the announcement of a triple lock by the Conservative/Liberal Democrat coalition government in its first budget in 2010. It had been a key promise in the Lib Dem manifesto, and it was implemented in 2011 by then-chancellor George Osborne.

Since 2011, the triple lock has increased the value of the state pension considerably. Analysis by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) showed that between 2010-2023, the median disposable household income for pensioners rose by 15%. Cross-party support for maintaining the triple lock during the 2019 general election demonstrated a broad commitment to the steady increase of the state pension.

However, while average incomes in later life have risen, the gap between poorer pensioners and those on average incomes has widened. Relative poverty among pensioners rose from 13% in 2011, to 16% in 2022. Thus, the triple lock has not necessarily meant that fewer? pensioners are living in poverty.

At the same time, the key safety net for low-income pensioners is not the state pension alone. Historically, this was provided by something called the minimum income guarantee. This is a means-tested benefit which ensures that pensioners’ weekly income does not fall below a legally set minimum (£238 per week for a single person in 2026/7, and £363.25 for a couple), which was also linked to earnings.

The minimum income guarantee was replaced by the guarantee element of pension credit (a means-tested benefit that tops up the income of poorer pensioners). This move towards some kind of guarantee of a minimum income didn’t come with the fanfare of the triple lock – but it did make a big difference to pensioners’ incomes before the triple lock was introduced.

The Resolution Foundation, an independent thinktank focused on raising UK living standards, estimated that there was a 15.8 percentage point fall in pensioner relative poverty between 1997-98 and 2011-12, as growing incomes for poor pensioners closed the gap with the non-pensioner median income.
But there are still an estimated 760,000 vulnerable pensioners who are eligible for means-tested pension credit, but who failed to claim it in 2025/6.

The government’s own analysis shows that this happens for a number of reasons: people may not have heard of it, or don’t know who to contact in order to claim it. The application process is complicated, and for some there may be stigma attached to claiming.

One solution to lifting more pensioners out of poverty might be increasing the value of pension credit and improving its take-up. It is notable that the triple lock does not apply to pension credit or to winter fuel payments, which use different criteria to work out the rate of increase.

Analysis by the IFS illustrates that the “new” triple lock, as outlined in Burnham’s speech, is still expected to generate an increase in the value of the state pension in the future. However, such increase will not permanently “ratchet up” the level of the state pension in the same way as the “old” triple lock.

articles.title: China and the EU could turn Morocco into a surprise global hub for electric vehicles
articles.author: Linda Calabrese, Senior Research Fellow in the International Economic Development Group, ODI Global
paras: China now makes more than seven in ten of the world’s electric cars. In 2024 it produced over 12 million, 1.25 million of which were exported, mainly to Europe.

The EU is worried about this – alarmed by cheap, state-subsidised Chinese vehicles flooding its market and threatening the 13 million jobs which depend on its own auto industry. So the bloc has spent the past two years building a system of tariffs and rules to keep Chinese cars at bay.
In 2024, it imposed extra duties of up to 35% on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs), on top of an existing 10% import tariff. So far though, the EU’s tactics have yielded limited results.
Chinese vehicle sales in Europe nearly doubled between 2024 and 2025.
And much of this sales volume is being driven by the EV powerhouse that is developing at speed in Morocco.
Chinese firms producing cars in Morocco avoid exposure to those EU tariffs, and have announced US$6 billion (£4.5 billion) of investment in battery and electric car component plants in the country.

As a production base, Morocco has plenty of other advantages too. Its deep-water port in Tangier is the largest in Africa and the Mediterranean. It is also surrounded by state-sponsored industrial zones built specifically for carmakers and their suppliers.
Like its neighbours, Morocco has a free trade agreement with the EU, but is the only north African country which has one with the US.
And crucially, it has a good supply of the critical minerals needed for making batteries for EVs, including around 70% of the world’s phosphate reserves and plenty of cobalt.

Nor is Morocco starting from scratch in the car manufacturing business. Cars are the country’s biggest export. Many Moroccan workers have been trained in automotive assembly thanks to two major car companies.

Renault and Stellantis (the owner of 14 car brands including Peugeot, Fiat and Alfa Romeo) form a manufacturing base in Morocco that exported US$17 billion in cars and parts in 2024. This made Morocco one of the EU’s largest automotive trading partners ahead of China.
Of the 560,000 vehicles Morocco produced in 2024, the vast majority were petrol and diesel models. Only around 50,000 were electric.

But a new wave of investment can help the industry shift to green. Recent multi-billion-euro commitments from Stellantis and Renault will expand EV and hybrid capacity. At the same time, Chinese investment is filling domestic gaps in cathode and battery cell production.
This transformation did not happen to Morocco by chance. The government has spent two decades laying the groundwork.

It has built “free zones”, areas where businesses can import, manufacture, process and re-export goods without paying normal taxes or customs duties. These include automotive “clusters”, including the Tanger “automotive city”.
This year, Morocco introduced a carbon tax to keep its exports compliant with EU rules.
So Morocco has been positioning itself to benefit from the EU tariffs. Whether Morocco actually gains from this boom depends on what kind of production Chinese firms undertake.

They could treat Morocco as a mere transit hub, sending goods through Morocco with minimal processing purely to evade tariffs. Brussels has already caught one such case, ruling in 2025 that aluminium wheels shipped from Morocco were being unfairly subsidised by Beijing.

Or they could do the opposite: build real factories, share technology, train local engineers and buy from Moroccan suppliers. This is what would turn the current boom into lasting green industrialisation, of the type that the African Union wants to encourage, linking African mineral reserves to clean-energy manufacturing.
But there are potential stumbling blocks which could prevent Morocco from benefiting from this new wave of investment in the long term.

First, the EU rules themselves may not last. Its tariffs on Chinese electric cars are set for only five years, and legal challenges are already underway. Second, the technology may remain in Chinese hands. And third, the geopolitical and climate context is so volatile that business plans could change very quickly.

On the plus side, Morocco has an established manufacturing footprint and government support. So the unintended consequences of EU trade policy could end up producing one of the biggest green industrialisation stories of the next decade.

articles.title: The oil market that sets today’s gas prices was invented in western Pennsylvania
articles.author: Brian C. Black, Distinguished Professor of History and Environmental Studies, Penn State
paras: The fall of 2026 is a moment of energy centrality, when geopolitics unfolding far away shows up in Americans’ everyday lives.
In Pennsylvania, the statewide diesel price averages US$6.50 per gallon. In Iowa, farmers are paying more than $6 a gallon for diesel. And in Alaska, unleaded gas runs more than $9 a gallon.

As a distinguished professor of history and environmental studies at Penn State Altoona, I write widely about oil and energy issues. This moment has me thinking about how the oil industry began nearly 170 years ago in northwestern Pennsylvania.
Setting crude prices in Oil City

In 1859, Edwin Drake struck oil along Oil Creek near Titusville, Pennsylvania. His well was funded by investors from New Bedford, Massachusetts, who were looking for a replacement for whale oil, which was expensive and challenging to acquire.

The first oil deals were struck on the streets of Oil City, about 90 miles north of Pittsburgh, while traders were still working out basic questions about “rock oil,” as crude was then called: What was it good for, and how much should it cost?

To create a more formal system, the oil traders developed a railroad car designed to be a rolling oil exchange on the Oil Creek Railway. It made 13 stops daily between Titusville and Oil City, and trading was conducted on the honor system, with no written certificates of purchase or sale.
As the industry quickly grew, an oil exchange office was set up in the Arlington Hotel in Oil City.

Traders pushed for a building of their own, arguing that a growing industry needed a more formal market. By 1874, Pennsylvania’s Oil Valley was producing roughly 30,000 barrels of crude oil a day, which sold for an average of about $1.15 a barrel.

Rather than physically moving barrels around, trading had moved from handshakes to paper. Pipelines issued certificates representing the oil in their lines. Traders bought and sold the paper certificates representing oil, often trading the same barrels many times in a single day. As a result, the volume of oil changing hands could reach 10 million to 14 million barrels a day, hundreds of times more than the wells actually produced.
In April 1874, a group of Oil City oil men received a state charter to form the Oil City Oil Exchange. Construction started in July 1877 at the corner of Center and Seneca streets.

When the Oil Exchange opened in April 1878, the local newspaper called it “the largest and most elaborate structure ever erected in the Oil Region.” The building, the paper said, reflected how big the speculative side of the oil trade had become. Standard Oil, the nation’s largest oil company at the time, owned by John D. Rockefeller, kept offices in the building.
The Oil City Oil Exchange heavily influenced early crude oil pricing. Brokers there collected 10 cents a barrel from buyers and 5 cents from sellers.

While the Oil City Oil Exchange was the center of the oil industry for nearly two decades, by 1895 Standard Oil had effectively cornered the market. Its chief buyer, Titusville resident Joseph Seep, began paying producers cash directly, at a price Standard set itself. That control lasted until 1911, when the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in a landmark antitrust case that the trust had to be broken into 34 separate companies.
After that, no single company controlled the price of crude oil.
Who sets the price of oil now
Predicting oil prices became a much bigger concern after the oil crises of the 1970s, when sudden price hikes rattled economies around the world.

Today, the price of crude oil is set largely by traders on two exchanges: the New York Mercantile Exchange and the Intercontinental Exchange. Prices there shift from second to second, and gas prices at the pump follow them, usually within days or weeks.

Much of that trading involves futures contracts, which are agreements to buy oil at a set price on a future date. In the U.S., the benchmark contract is for oil delivered to Cushing, Oklahoma, a storage hub where many of the country’s pipelines meet.

The latest shock to that system began this year. War began on Feb. 28, 2026, when the U.S. and Israel launched airstrikes on Iranian military targets that killed Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Iran struck back with missiles and drones and began attacking commercial ships in the waters around the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula that connects the Persian Gulf to the open ocean.
Within days, the attacks and a wave of canceled shipping insurance brought tanker traffic nearly to a halt.

On March 2, a Revolutionary Guard commander made the closure official in a statement carried by Iran’s state media: “The Strait of Hormuz is closed. If anyone tries to pass, the heroes of the Revolutionary Guards and the regular navy will set those ships ablaze.”
Roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil normally passes through the strait. Most of it goes to Asia, not the U.S. But because oil is traded on a global market, prices rose everywhere.

Oil and gas prices kept climbing as peace talks failed. By May 2026, the average price of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. was 50% higher than before the war began. Since then, Gulf oil producers have found ways around the blockade, sending oil through pipelines to ports outside the strait and through a U.S.-guarded shipping route near Oman. By late September, those work-arounds had restored about half of the oil that normally passes through the strait, helping keep crude prices around $100 a barrel instead of the much higher levels many analysts had feared.

Oil City’s exchange building is long gone. It was torn down in 1926 to make way for a bank. But the market its traders built, where paper claims on oil change hands far faster than the oil itself moves, still sets what drivers pay at the pump in Oil City and everywhere else.

articles.title: Why your boss matters more than remote or hybrid work when it comes to burnout and job satisfaction
articles.author: Christos Makridis, Associate Research Professor of Information Systems, Arizona State University; Institute for Humane Studies
paras: The post-pandemic push to bring workers back to the office has left many nostalgic for more flexible arrangements, such as hybrid or remote work.

But a wealth of data since the pandemic now suggests that workplace factors like feeling appreciated and having a good relationship with your manager are much more tied to job satisfaction than the actual time spent in the office.

To understand this insight, it’s important to recognize that a return to the office can mean very different things to different workers. Someone who values uninterrupted time at home may resent the commute. A younger trainee struggling to learn the job may welcome easier access to colleagues. An employee who dislikes their manager may lament having to see them in person.
These differences help explain why the return-to-office debate often produces conflicting answers.

As a researcher of the ways technology is changing the workplace, I co-authored a study with business and accounting scholar Jason Schloetzer that analyzed responses from nearly 165,000 U.S. employees between 2020 and 2023 from the database Payscale. These surveys let us look beyond location to ask whether employees felt appreciated; considered pay fair and transparent; received useful communication; had chances to develop; and enjoyed a good relationship with their manager.

Once we accounted for these and other job-specific variables, we found that the edge in satisfaction for fully or mostly remote workers disappears. The only group of employees who felt more satisfied on the job were those who sometimes worked remotely – and that difference was modest.
In other words, long-standing factors shaping job satisfaction outweighed workplace format when it came to making employees happy.
The workplace behind the work arrangement
Semi- or fully remote workers may appear more satisfied. But other factors, such as having better pay or more supportive workplace practices, need to be taken into account, we argue.

Employees’ relationships with their managers is one of those variables. We asked employees to rate the statement “I have a great relationship with my direct manager” on a 5-point scale, with 4 or 5 indicating favorable. The measure reflects the employee’s own assessment rather than a checklist of managerial skills; questions about communication, appreciation and development opportunities were asked separately.

A favorable manager relationship was tied to higher job satisfaction across work arrangements, we found. But that association was stronger among employees working on-site than among those who always or sometimes worked remotely. One possible explanation is that working together gives employees more opportunities to benefit from a supportive manager who mentors and offers development opportunities, while distance can offer some relief when the relationship is less favorable.

We also used data from the Gallup Workplace Panel to study the same workers over time. These results reinforced our findings: It’s important to consider the workplace as a whole when evaluating remote or hybrid work.
Burnout and happiness are different questions

Feeling satisfied with a job, however, doesn’t necessarily mean feeling well overall. Someone can like their job while feeling exhausted, or they may appreciate working at home while feeling socially disconnected. That’s why we treat job satisfaction, burnout and happiness as separate values, and why we distinguish stress on a particular day from persistent work exhaustion.

Looking at stress, for example, we found that it’s common across work arrangements. According to Gallup’s 2026 State of the Global Workplace report, 41% of fully remote employees reported substantial stress the previous day, compared with 46% of hybrid employees, as well as 46% of on-site employees whose jobs could be done remotely.

Feeling satisfied with a job, however, doesn’t necessarily mean feeling well overall. Someone can value their work while finding its demands exhausting. Job satisfaction, daily stress and burnout capture different aspects of that experience.

Physicians are one example. Among physicians whose organizations participated in an American Medical Association survey in 2024, about three-quarters reporting being satisfied with their job, while almost half reported feeling a great deal of stress because of their job, such as from burdensome paperwork or staff shortages.
The published summary doesn’t identify exactly how many doctors reported both, but it shows that satisfaction and widespread stress can coexist within a profession.

Meanwhile, separate Gallup research on nearly 7,500 full-time U.S. employees helps explain why working conditions deserve attention. The factors most closely tied to burnout included unfair treatment, crushing workloads, unclear expectations, poor communication and support from managers, and unreasonable deadlines.

Work location may ease some pressures while introducing others. Working from home can remove a draining commute, for example, while making it harder to get timely help from colleagues. But neither arrangement automatically resolves an excessive workload or uncertainty about manager expectations.
Those problems require attention wherever employees work.
Working apart can carry social costs
The expression “work-life balance” implies that it’s healthy to engage in social activity with friends and family outside work.

But as other research of mine shows, more flexibility for office work doesn’t necessarily translate into more time with other people. Among younger workers in occupations that can readily be done remotely, I found that the share of leisure time spent alone rose from about 25% to 40% from 2017 to 2024. For workers who also spend their workday alone, that means fewer opportunities for socializing both on and off the job.

Time alone doesn’t have to lead to loneliness. But the finding raises a concern: Just because you gain more control over your schedule doesn’t mean that friends, family or colleagues will be available to share that time – or that you’ll make the effort to see them.

Related research suggests that these concerns about social connection deserve more attention. The expansion of remote work has been tied to increases in isolation and mental distress, according to new research published by economists Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington and Amanda Pallais. In a nonrandomized experiment covering almost 600,000 people, they compared changes in mental health before and after the pandemic in jobs that could and could not readily be done remotely, excluding 2020 and 2021. Remote workers living alone fared the worst.
These findings raise a practical question for employers: How can time together at work become more useful?

For employers considering a return to the office, a useful starting point is to first identify what employees gain from being together and then organize office time around it. Teams that depend on frequent collaboration need overlapping schedules. Newer employees need access to colleagues who can teach them. Managers need to provide useful feedback and address workload issues wherever people work, and employees need to be responsive to managerial efforts to engage them.

Employee preferences and job requirements differ across organizations, so managers need to determine which arrangements suit their teams. But regular, useful feedback matters across on-site, hybrid and remote settings. That means discussing priorities, recognizing employees’ contributions and helping them work effectively with colleagues.
As Gallup workplace researcher Jim Harter has suggested, this kind of feedback should become a weekly habit.
“These conversations don’t have to be long; 15 to 30 minutes, done consistently, is enough,” he wrote.

Christos Makridis is also a senior researcher in Gallup, receives funding from foundations to study remote work and organizations, and is affiliated with other nonprofit education and thinktank institutions.

articles.title: Energy price cap: the cost of your coffee could be about to go up
articles.author: Giray Gozgor, Associate Professor of Economics & Finance, School of Management, University of Bradford
paras: This autumn, the cost of gas and electricity for a typical UK household is expected to rise from £1,663 to £1,723 a year.

The change, due to higher wholesale gas prices, will be easy enough to spot on a household bill. But those rising costs can also affect people in less obvious ways, through the price of a coffee, for example, or a pub lunch or haircut.
That’s because the energy price cap – which limits the unit rates suppliers can charge – applies only to households on certain tariffs. It does not apply to the energy bills of small businesses.
Many cafes, bakeries, pubs and shops arrange their own energy contracts with suppliers, either directly or through a broker, sometimes fixing the unit price for several years.

What each business pays depends on the type of contract and the deal it secures. And not all businesses will be affected at the same time. Two cafes, for example, operating on the same high street, might be using similar ovens, fridges, coffee machines and lighting. But if one signed a fixed energy contract last year, and the other has a contract that ends next month, their overall costs could soon look very different.

The first cafe may remain protected from higher wholesale prices under its existing contract for quite a while. The second faces current market conditions when arranging its next deal, and could receive a higher renewal quote.
The two businesses can therefore be paying very different energy bills despite using roughly the same amount of electricity.

A contract negotiation can work in the other direction, of course. A business that fixed its price near the peak of a previous energy price crisis may end up receiving a cheaper offer when it renews. The timing of a contract, its duration and the rate previously agreed all help determine whether renewal brings an increase or a saving.

But if a cafe receives a higher renewal quote, it cannot simply stop using its fridge or coffee machine. And it may have little scope to switch its use of power to times of day when energy is cheaper. Customers want coffee in the morning and meals at lunchtime.
So the owner is left with a short list of difficult options. They can raise prices, accept lower profits, reduce staff hours and opening times or postpone other spending.

Some will decide on a mix of these responses. Research shows that during previous energy price shocks, profitability declined for many UK firms. This suggests that businesses absorbed some of the higher costs rather than passing them on in full to customers.
But for a company operating on a narrow margin, even a small increase in the cost of doing business can force a visible change.

And this is one of the reasons why this inflation rate can linger more broadly. Businesses do not all face higher energy costs at the same time. Some face an immediate increase in their energy bills, while others experience it when their fixed contracts expire.

As these contracts come up for renewal at different times, higher energy costs can gradually feed through into the prices customers pay. Official figures show that around 60% of UK firms have fixed-price gas and electricity contracts, meaning that higher energy costs can take time to feed through fully.

In August 2026, the annual rate of inflation in restaurants and hotels was higher (4.1%) than the general UK inflation rate (3.1%). Energy costs are one of several factors influencing higher prices in the hospitality sector.
Today’s menu prices may partly reflect energy contracts signed months ago, while future prices can reflect deals being negotiated now.

And while the household price cap is updated every three months (and until March 2027 will be accompanied by the removal of VAT from electricity), energy contracts for businesses follow thousands of separate calendars. When renewal brings higher costs, owners must decide how much they can absorb and how much they can pass on to customers.

But even an eventual fall in wholesale energy prices will take time to lower businesses’ costs. And it may just slow down further price increases rather than lead to cheaper refreshments on the highly pressured high street.

articles.title: Coolcations: tourism boom is taking a toll on chillier destinations
articles.author: Mehri Khosravi, Energy and Carbon Senior Research Fellow, University of East London; United Nations University
paras: Rising numbers of visitors headed for destinations in northern Europe in the summer of 2026, seeking respite from the heat.
For years, summer holidays in Europe have followed a familiar pattern: head south in search of sunshine. But climate change is beginning to turn that logic on its head.
As temperatures rise across southern Europe, traditionally popular destinations are facing increasingly difficult summer conditions, from extreme hot temperatures to wildfires and water shortages.

Rather than abandoning summer travel, some tourists are beginning to change the destinations they want to spend time in. The trend has even acquired a name: the “coolcation”. For an individual traveller, this can be a sensible response to rising temperatures. A cooler destination can make outdoor activities more comfortable and allow people to continue taking summer holidays while avoiding the most intense heat.

For northern European destinations, this could look like an opportunity. Northern Europe (defined as Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Sweden and the UK) recorded a 10% increase in visitor numbers between April and June 2026, compared with the same period in 2025, according to the European Travel Commission.

One travel agent reported seeing a rise in searches for cooler destinations rise by 74% compared with 2025. Meanwhile, a travel app, Polarsteps, launched a summer heat escape index, analysing the temperatures at 25 destinations, after it carried out a survey finding that 35% of British travellers had chosen a cooler summer destination in 2026.

But if enough people make the same decision, a destination that was attractive partly because it was cooler, quieter or less crowded can begin to experience the crowds associated with mass tourism, and potentially an environmental cost.

The individual traveller is adapting successfully to climate change by moving away from heat. But that adaptation can redistribute tourism pressure towards destinations that may have less capacity to absorb it.
Going to Scotland for its weather
Scotland provides a useful example.

National tourism agency VisitBritain reported that flight bookings for Scottish destinations made during the six weeks ending mid-July rose 15%, compared with the same period in 2025. At the same time bookings for London, which was experiencing an extremely hot summer, dropped.

Although Scotland also experienced hotter weather than usual at times, and did experience wildfires in the Cairngorms, it was far cooler than London and the south of England. The early indications are that Scotland has seen a growth in tourism in 2026.
Some popular Scottish destinations, such as Glencoe, opened additional infrastructure in 2026, including a new car park, to cope with expanding numbers of tourists.
What are the environmental implications?
Growing tourism can bring employment, spending and investment. However, increasing visitor numbers also creates pressure on housing, infrastructure, public services and natural environments.

Some Scottish communities already perceive tourism as putting considerable pressure on local areas. In 2025, 32% of Highland and 48% of Orkney residents felt tourism placed too much pressure on their area, compared with 8% across Scotland. Edinburgh has recently introduced a 5% tourist tax on the first five nights of any stay, which can be used to help fund local infrastructure and housing projects.

Norway is also seeing similar trends. The number of nights international guests booked into Norwegian hotels increased by 3.2% between May and July 2026, compared with the same period in 2025, rising from 3.28 million to 3.39 million. Norway has also introduced a new tax, allowing local councils experiencing tourism pressure to charge up to 3% on tourist accommodation.
In Rovaniemi, a city in Finnish Lapland, rising winter tourism has increased pressure on housing and local services.
As with other tourist centres, renting out accommodation to tourists has reduced housing availability for local people and contributed to rising rents.
Coolcations may represent more than a change in holiday preference. They may become part of a wider redistribution of climate-related tourism pressure.
Around 76% of Europeans say climate-related factors now influence their travel behaviour. Among those adapting their plans, 16% are looking for destinations with milder temperatures.

But there are environmental costs. Visitors who spend time in a wild and rural environment can lead to damage such as trampling, soil compaction and erosion. Increased human presence can also disturb wildlife and damage vegetation. This can be particularly pronounced in mountain and remote locations, where ecosystems are often fragile.

Coolcations may add a new climate-driven layer to pressures that already exist. The challenge for northern European destinations is to anticipate how climate change could reshape tourism demand before infrastructure, housing and natural environments become overwhelmed.

articles.title: Why older lawmakers may wait too long to step aside
articles.author: Nancy Forster-Holt, Clinical Associate Professor of Innovation and Entrepreneurship, University of Rhode Island
paras: U.S. Sen. Ed Markey is 80 and has served in Congress for half a century. His Democratic primary challenger in Massachusetts, U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, is 47 and made generational change a centerpiece of his campaign. Markey won the Sept. 1, 2026, primary anyway by nearly 30 percentage points.

He’s not the only octogenarian to prevail in a competitive primary in 2026. Eleven won their primaries and are on the ballot for the 2026 midterm elections. The oldest primary winner was Sen. Jim Risch of Idaho, an 83-year-old Republican.
It seems to be an issue both major political parties agree on: For many candidates, age is just a number, even when it starts with an 8 or a 9.

My colleagues and I study succession in family-run businesses and other occupations where leadership, identity and longevity can become deeply intertwined. Whether someone is in charge of a company or is a lawmaker, their work does not only keep them busy. It provides status, an identity and a sense of mission. Letting go means giving up more than a job.
When business leaders or politicians linger for too long, it can be costly for their companies or constituents because potential successors may become frustrated by waiting and decide to move on.

When any kind of leader remains in their role for decades, underlying reasons can range from a genuine love for what they do to not knowing what they will do – or who they will be – once they leave. However, waiting too long can mean they’ll have to hand off their responsibilities in crisis mode.
In family businesses, my research team found, the people closest to their leaders – including relatives, employees and longtime supporters – may go quiet rather than press the issue.
This dynamic is not limited to the business world. It also applies to many of the older members of Congress.
A closer look at the large numbers of legislators who continue to serve during their golden years reflects two trends.
First, many are elected for the first time when they’re middle-aged. New House members were about 50 years old and new senators around 55 in 2025.

Second, although the median age of House lawmakers is now about 60, and 66 in the Senate, there’s a small group of long-serving members who remain in office into and past their 80s and keep running for reelection.
Seeing the advantages of ‘not yet’
Every lawmaker can have a reason to say “not yet.” So can their staff members, who may be loyal to them and their missions and professionally invested in the work they have built together.

Political parties value the electoral advantages of incumbents, while constituents may value the seniority, relationships and influence that come with having spent decades serving in Congress. And incumbents can sincerely believe important work remains unfinished.
However, unusually prolonged service in any position increases the possibility that illness, cognitive decline or death will lead to an unplanned and probably rocky transition.
What’s more, when politicians serve into their late 70s, 80s or beyond, they are breaking with ordinary employment patterns.
The typical American retires in their early 60s, with two-thirds of U.S. workers exiting the labor force before their 65th birthday.
Setting good and bad examples
There are examples of long-serving politicians choosing to plan their exit closer to standard retirement age.

One is Barbara Boxer. After more than three decades in Congress, the 74-year-old California Democrat announced in January 2015 that she would not seek reelection to the U.S. Senate the following year. “There is a time when you want the next generation to step in and step up,” she said.

Boxer’s early decision gave prospective successors nearly two years to organize and voters the opportunity to choose among them. Kamala Harris won the seat but stepped away to serve as President Joe Biden’s vice president.

This departure offers a striking contrast with that of Boxer’s longtime colleague, Sen. Dianne Feinstein, who remained in the Senate through a lengthy health-related absence in 2023. Feinstein, also a California Democrat, died in office that September. She was 90 years old.

She served on the influential Senate Judiciary Committee, which considers federal judicial nominations, including Supreme Court nominees. During her nearly three-month absence, the committee was deadlocked on dozens of Biden nominations after Republicans refused to let the Democrats appoint a temporary replacement for her and she refused to step down.
The tragic way Feinstein’s storied political career ended illustrated what can go wrong when lawmakers keep saying “not yet” until it’s too late.

That turned out to be the case with Biden, who reluctantly ended his presidential reelection campaign in July 2024. However, several books published since then include details about how his inner circle initially advised him to run again.
A rushed attempt at succession followed Biden’s abrupt withdrawal from the race. Harris became the Democratic nominee without participating in any of the 2024 primaries.
When change finally came, it arrived under duress rather than by design. And Harris lost the election to Donald Trump.

U.S. Rep. Kay Granger, a Texas Republican, announced in 2023 that she would not seek reelection the following year. It soon became clear that severe health problems were preventing her from serving her constituents.

The former House Appropriations Committee chair didn’t cast a vote in her final six months in office for a good reason: She had dementia and was staying in a Texas assisted-living facility that provided memory care services to some residents. Granger died in August 2026 at 83.

U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, a former Senate majority and minority leader, has announced that he will step down when his current term – the Kentucky Republican’s seventh – ends in January 2027. But a fall, hospitalization and subsequent stint in a rehabilitation center in mid-2026 prompted renewed public scrutiny of the 84-year-old’s health and ability to complete his term.

U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, who turned 93 on Sept. 17, 2026, and appears to be in good health, has not yet said whether he’s running for a ninth six-year term in 2028. But the Republican, who is the oldest person serving in Congress, has urged his constituents to vote for a Republican for governor.
“I don’t plan on dying in office, but if I did, I don’t want a Democratic governor choosing my successor,” Grassley said at a political event in Des Moines in late September 2026.
Learning from palliative care
My colleagues and I found an unlikely way to think differently about leadership transitions: considering lessons about letting go from palliative care.

Leaving political office or another leadership role, of course, is not the same as dying. But, as is true before someone develops a terminal medical condition, advance planning is most useful while people can still articulate what matters to them and exercise meaningful choices about what comes next.

I’ve learned that it’s a mistake to treat succession as something to discuss only when a leader must move on for health or other reasons. So, in addition to my work as a management professor, and to inform my research, as well as the workshops I hold for aging business owners and members of their inner circles, I have been trained as an end-of-life doula. I decided to do this because I lacked the vocabulary and tools that facilitated difficult conversations and decisions about their legacy and what is important to the leader as they let go.
Palliative care supports the act of letting go long before death – the same challenge confronting business leaders and the companies they run.

When voters consider whether to vote for an aging incumbent, they may wonder whether that lawmaker is already too old for their demanding job or soon will be. But that may be the wrong question. It might be better to ask whether the legislators who represent you, no matter their age, have a plan for letting go.

articles.title: Fewer Americans are getting help buying groceries from SNAP benefits as states grapple with the program’s cascade of changes
articles.author: Tracy Roof, Associate Professor of Political Science, University of Richmond
paras: The number of people enrolled in the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program is falling fast. The program formerly known as food stamps helped roughly 42 million Americans put food on the table in 2025.

As of June 2026, the most recent data available, the number of people enrolled in the program in the whole country had declined by almost 13% to 36.4 million. Among those no longer getting benefits are an estimated 1.5 million children.
What explains this decline?
President Donald Trump says a strong economy has driven down demand for the program.

It’s possible that some people have left the program because their incomes rose. But the enrollment decline has a lot to do with the big tax-and-spending package the president signed into law in July 2025.
States are struggling to keep up
For example, the law caused some immigrants residing legally in the country, such as refugees and those seeking asylum, to no longer be eligible for SNAP benefits.

In addition, more people enrolled in SNAP now may only get up to three months of benefits if they don’t work, engage in training programs or volunteer at least 80 hours a month. These work requirements previously applied only to adults up to the age of 54; that cutoff is rising to 64. Another change is that parents of older children ages 14-17 are now expected to meet these work requirements.

All states are phasing in these restrictions, but the number of people getting SNAP benefits is falling much faster in some states than others. That includes Arizona, where enrollment has fallen by almost half, along with Louisiana and Illinois, where it’s down by about one-fifth.
And now, states must pay more to run SNAP, which is federally funded but state-administered.

In my research on the history of SNAP, I’ve found that changes in the way states run their programs have a big impact on who can get help. States are struggling to adapt to new federal policies. As additional changes roll out, more families may lose access to SNAP.
Covering more of the administrative costs

As of Oct. 1, 2026, states have to pay 75% of all administrative costs, which include paying staff who manage the enrollment process and maintaining the program’s computer systems. Previously, states paid 50% of those costs. The federal government estimates that states and local governments will pay roughly US$17 billion more in administrative costs over the next five years.

In the 2027 fiscal year, which began on Oct. 1, California – with the largest population of any state – will be responsible for paying roughly $670 million more to run the program. Wyoming, with the smallest number of residents, will pay about $3 million more.
Costs will be shifted to local governments in nine of the 10 states where SNAP is administered by counties.
Looming changes tied to ‘payment error rates’

State agencies and some state legislatures are imposing stricter rules and requiring applicants to provide more paperwork documenting their income, expenses and the number of people in their household.
Caseworkers in states such as Arizona have reportedly been overwhelmed with the paperwork. Those seeking help have spent hours trying to get through on phone lines and have faced monthslong delays.

States are taking these steps to get ready for another change that will roll out in October 2027. At that point, many states will also have to cover up to 15% of the costs of benefits for the first time since the program began in the 1960s.
This cost is much larger than the administrative costs and could be staggering for many states.

How much a state pays will be based on its “payment error rate.” These error rates measure how much in benefits are paid above or below what families are actually entitled to based on their household size, income and expenses. It is calculated based on an in-depth review of a small sample of a state’s benefits payments each year.

These inaccurate payments are generally a result of mistakes on the part of the applicant or their caseworker – they rarely are the result of fraud. The payment error rate includes benefits paid to ineligible participants. It does not include payments never made to applicants who were eligible for benefits but wrongly denied them or incorrectly dropped from the program.
Supporters of SNAP argue that this makes states err on the side of denying benefits.
States with an error rate less than 6% won’t face new costs for benefits. But only nine states had rates that low in 2025.

States with an error rate between 6% and 8% will be responsible for 5% of the costs of their residents’ SNAP benefits. States with an error rate between 8% and 10% will have to cover 10%. States with error rates over 10% will have to cover 15%.

There’s a weird twist: If a state has an error rate over 13.32%, it won’t have to pay part of the cost of residents’ SNAP benefits for up to two years as they would have had it been in the 6% to 13.32% range.
Farm bill politics could play a role

To reduce their error rates, states need to invest in more staff, training, technology and better application and verification procedures. But states had little time to do all that. The states’ share of costs slated to kick in as of October 2027 is based on the error rates in the fiscal year that ended in September 2026.
Organizations representing state and local governments and social workers are pushing for an across-the board two-year delay.

What’s more, legislation known as the “farm bill,” which sets policies for agriculture, conservation and food-related assistance like SNAP, is now ensnared in the dispute. Democrats, whose support is needed to pass the legislation in the Senate, would like to see most of the new SNAP changes repealed.
Congress aims to pass a farm bill roughly every five years, but the most recent one, which was finalized in 2018, has expired.

Short of rolling back all the SNAP policy changes, many Democrats have refused to vote for the farm bill unless it includes a two-year delay for all states in shouldering part of the cost of SNAP benefits.
If the Democratic Party holds a majority in one or both chambers of Congress after the 2026 midterm elections, their leverage could increase in these negotiations.

The Republican Party’s version of the farm bill now pending in the Senate includes a one-year delay in the benefits-funding changes. But it would increase the states’ burden even more than the policy planned for October 2027. That’s a nonstarter for Democrats.
What states can do about all this

Meanwhile, there are many signs that a large share of the people who have lost their SNAP benefits are struggling to feed their families. More people, for example, are seeking help from food pantries and banks, which fear they will not be able to keep up with growing demand.
It’s hard to predict what might happen next.
SNAP’s higher costs could force states and counties to raise taxes, cut spending on other programs or find ways to reduce spending on SNAP.
Officials in some states are saying that they may find they need to drop the program altogether.

Because states lack the authority to change benefit amounts or do much to directly limit who qualifies for the program, I believe more states will be tempted to add red tape to lower their error rates, reduce the number of people getting benefits, or both.

articles.title: Why it’s more important than ever to jump-start entrepreneurial careers from the college classroom
articles.author: Raghupathy Sivakumar, Vice President of Commercialization and Chief Commercialization Officer, Georgia Institute of Technology
paras: Recent college graduates are facing a job market that’s only getting tougher. Their unemployment rate hit 5.7%, compared to 4.1% for all workers, in June 2026. That may not sound like much, but it’s one of the worst rates in the past 20 years.
Meanwhile, roughly 4 in 10 graduates are underemployed, which means they work in jobs that typically don’t require a college degree. That’s the highest rate since the COVID-19 pandemic.

As an educator for more than 25 years, I see the growing anxiety every day. In a change from years past, parents are now peppering me with questions: How can their kids leverage their college education in such a fast-changing world? Will they learn skills in school that will soon be antiquated once they graduate?

What’s essential to understand is that technology adoption cycles have accelerated at a breathtaking rate over the past few years. While the telephone and television took decades to reach 100 million users, ChatGPT and TikTok attained that threshold in a matter of months. Colleges need to adapt their curricula accordingly.

Georgia Tech, where I teach engineering, has focused on pushing entrepreneurship across our campus since 2014. We’re seeing encouraging signs from our follow-ups with graduating students that it’s helping their early careers.

I believe one of the best ways to adjust to these changes is to embed entrepreneurial experiences throughout college. Such hands-on learning, in turn, develops versatile, adaptable talent, producing graduates who can pivot across jobs as industries, technologies and opportunities evolve. And this needn’t be confined to business students – young people in all majors can benefit.

The educational value of entrepreneurship isn’t principally that every student will be able to start a company. It’s that entrepreneurial experiences develop the capabilities students need in a rapidly changing economy – and ultimately build more resilient careers.
Here are some ways educators can future-proof the college experience, based on what I’ve learned and applied at Georgia Tech.

Making adaptability a core skill: Students need to learn how to be nimble. This means recognizing important changes in the landscape, identifying new problems and the opportunities they create, articulating a response and mobilizing the necessary resources. Ultimately, this approach will help students be prepared for the real world.

To impart these lessons, I believe colleges should provide hands-on opportunities to help students learn through experience before they enter the workforce. For example, they could encourage students to develop a business venture idea that addresses a newly created opportunity in the marketplace through accelerators, or short-term “boot camps” for young companies to help them grown quickly. One example is Greptile, a startup that came out of the Georgia Tech CREATE-X accelerator.
The goal isn’t that a startup will be launched – that depends on several factors coming together – but that the student gains the experience to understand a changing landscape.

Understanding customer value: Colleges can also teach students how to think about customer value – namely, why the solution they’re working on matters to the consumers buying it. This isn’t just for business students. All students can gain from learning to think about the customers or clients they will deal with in their careers. In fact, students from 38 majors have participated in the entrepreneurship programs at Georgia Tech.

Through on-the-ground experience that requires them to find customers, students can learn about the real-world impact of the products and services they create. When students spend hundreds of hours selling their young startup to the outside world, they learn to understand value at a deep level.

Emphasizing fundamentals: Fundamental skills are key because they outlast the technology underpinning the business. In fact, the more quickly specific technologies change, the more important a strong grounding in fundamentals becomes. This means it’s a smarter investment to offer, say, a fundamental course on wireless networking or deep learning concepts over a course that teaches specific wireless technologies or emphasizes the use of a specific model. A strong foundation gives students the tools to adapt to technologies that may not yet exist when they graduate.
The many paths toward entrepreneurship
Another great advantage of entrepreneurial experiences is that they force students to deal with uncertainty, recognize opportunities, work around resource constraints and learn how to create value.

But other strategies work as well. A few examples are project-based learning, internships and interdisciplinary capstone classes that let students pursue independent research projects as their final course.

That said, entrepreneurial experiences provide an unusually concentrated and effective environment that requires students to solve problems, engage with customers and mobilize resources they don’t directly control – all while getting real-world feedback.

More and more universities and colleges understand this point and have ramped up support for entrepreneurial activity for their students, such as Cornell and the University of Washington. At Georgia Tech, we have a playbook that we have developed through our experiences that follows the following principles:

Embed entrepreneurship into the curriculum: One simple way for colleges to incorporate entrepreneurial experiences into their coursework is to offer an entrepreneurship minor to all students, regardless of major. This would offer the opportunity to a broader range of students who otherwise might miss out.

Build a pathway to business creation: Entrepreneurial education is most effective when it leads to something bigger. To that end, many colleges are now offering a startup accelerator, including MIT, Rice University and the University of Texas.

But more is needed: A startup pathway that caters to students at all stages can substantially broaden participation and impact, regardless of whether a business results. At Georgia Tech, we have a learn/make/launch/scale pathway that offers programs and resources for learning about entrepreneurship, building solutions, launching new ventures and eventually scaling them.

Offer real venture experience: A successful model combines theoretical learning with hands-on experience. The confidence that students gain through that experience may be at least as important an educational outcome as the viability of the startups they launch. After all, since most startups tend to fail, confidence is a value that successful entrepreneurs have to sustain.
Transferring skills to the workforce

There’s another important element that’s needed: private sector partnerships. Fortunately, entrepreneurial education is well aligned with the interests of universities’ traditional corporate partners.

These companies, especially those with established, successful business models, are eager to hire students with a strong understanding of fundamentals and entrepreneurial confidence. This next generation can help the companies navigate the future.

Companies can also offer industry know-how, mentorship opportunities and financial and in-kind support. And they understand that students building a startup have to think beyond their own discipline to succeed. For example, an engineering student will need to understand customers, pricing, finance, sales, operations, intellectual property and team building. That broader perspective can make them more effective when they enter a corporate environment full time.

The same capabilities can also translate into venture creation itself: The value of entrepreneurial education can be seen across both traditional workforce pathways and startup outcomes. Our experience at Georgia Tech offers evidence of both.

Startups launched by Georgia Tech students over the past decade have crossed US$4.5 billion in aggregate total valuation and have created thousands of jobs. We’ve also found encouraging early evidence that students who gain confidence through these experiences have stronger career outcomes.

Georgia Tech isn’t alone. The University System of Georgia has recently created a new role: a chief innovation and entrepreneurial strategies officer to lead an initiative across all of the state’s public colleges and universities.

Other universities are pursuing similar paths, including the University of Virginia, Rice University and Cornell University. All now have an institutionwide leadership position focused on entrepreneurship.

Taken together, these developments suggest that educators increasingly view entrepreneurship as more than just support for students who want to start companies. These steps will help ensure that when students walk across the stage to receive their diplomas, they can meet the challenges ahead of them.

articles.title: Does increased childcare funding help mothers into work?
articles.author: Eva Lloyd, Emeritus Professor of Early Childhood, School of Childhood and Social Care, University of East London
paras: Since Labour won the 2024 general election, policy focused on children in the early years – from birth to school age – and their parents has moved sharply up the political agenda.

The government’s most expensive early years commitment so far has been its decision to honour the previous administration’s pledge to provide 30 funded hours of childcare for children aged from nine months to school age whose parents are in work. This was implemented in September 2025.

If parents require their children to be in childcare for more than 30 hours a week (they might need over 50 hours to cover full-time employment), they pay the excess. Childcare providers may also charge for services on top of the funded hours, such as meals, nappies and optional activities. However, such charges cannot be mandatory conditions of accessing the funded hours.

The £9 billion allocated to this provision represents a doubling of childcare funding since 2024. The policy’s central aim is to make childcare more affordable for working parents and to increase mothers’ employment rates. It is also intended to support children’s development and educational outcomes.
We set out to explore whether increasing the funding for this system would increase mothers’ employment.

We compared England with South Korea, where a fairly similar arrangement has been on offer for a number of years. In Korea, though, early childhood education and care receives significantly higher funding. It stands at 0.9% of GDP, compared with 0.5% in the UK.

Korea has offered a universal entitlement of 35 hours of funded childcare weekly for children aged from birth to age two since 2012. This was extended to children aged three to five the following year.

Our study found systemic problems in both countries. Our findings suggest that the design of funding systems, and how they interact with labour market and parental leave policies, may matter more than funding levels alone.

England and Korea share similar early years policy goals. Both aim to support children’s development while helping mothers into work. Both also rely heavily on marketised childcare systems, meaning that different childcare providers compete to offer care. Both systems combine public, private for-profit and not-for-profit providers.

Public spending on early childhood education and care is proportionally much higher in Korea. Yet full-time maternal employment rates in Korea (56.2% in 2021) remain well below both UK (74.2% in 2021) and OECD averages (71.4% in 2021).

Possible explanations for the relatively low maternal employment levels may be found beyond the childcare funding model, in wider social and labour market conditions. In Korea, traditional gender norms and limited access to flexible, family-friendly employment practices such as paid maternity leave and flexible hours, continue to create major barriers to mothers returning to work. These issues are coupled with a wider gender pay gap.

At the same time, the childcare system itself faces structural weaknesses. Childcare provision hasn’t expanded enough to allow all children access to high-quality care, particularly in the private for-profit sectors.

In England, family-friendly employment policies, including maternity, paternity and parental leave, provide stronger support for maternal employment. But England’s childcare system also faces serious challenges.

Access and affordability problems persist. In some disadvantaged areas, “childcare deserts” mean families have no local access to good-quality childcare. With Korea, England shares the problems of limited provision for disadvantaged children, especially those with special educational needs and disabilities. In both countries, there is a problem of low pay and high staff turnover in the private-for-profit childcare sector.
Quality in England also varies considerably. The dominance of private for-profit provision, notably large childcare corporations, shapes staff pay, qualifications and working conditions.

The early years sector has problems recruiting workers and keeping them in the profession. Between 2018 and 2025, the number of registered childcare providers dropped by nearly 20%. Complex governance arrangements often leave parents confused about eligibility and access to subsidies.
These barriers affect English mothers’ ability to participate in paid work, particularly full-time work.
In both England and Korea, despite the funded hours, families may not be able to access high-quality childcare.

A 2025 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) report argues that investment in early childhood education and care can reduce social inequalities of the kind seen in both England and Korea. But it also stresses that how governments allocate funding matters.

Earlier comparative research reached similar conclusions. This research found that the distribution of childcare support can be as important as the scale of spending itself if disadvantaged children are to benefit.
In countries where reforms have combined affordability with guaranteed access to childcare, increases in mothers’ employment have been more evident.

From the 1970s, childcare expansion in Norway has had a demonstrable effect on mothers’ employment and working patterns. Germany’s more recent childcare expansion policies achieved similar outcomes. Both countries have streamlined systems of integrated early education and childcare, while parents pay income related fees. In some German states all places are free, while in Norway they are free for low-income families. In both countries children have a legal right to a nursery place from the age of one, whether or not their parents are in work.
Both England and Korea now appear close to important childcare policy “tipping points” where radical intervention is indicated.

In England, further progress is likely to depend on extending 30-hours childcare support beyond working families, simplifying complex subsidy arrangements, and strengthening regulation of childcare markets.

In Korea, improvements in maternal employment rates will primarily require the development of stronger family-friendly employment policies, and wider efforts to challenge persistent gender inequalities in both the workplace and family life.

The wider lesson is clear. Increased spending alone is unlikely to raise maternal employment if labour market structures, gender norms and childcare market dynamics remain unchanged. Both countries illustrate the limitations of heavily marketised childcare systems in delivering high-quality and sustainable early years provision that is accessible to all. Increasing childcare funding cannot be separated from employment policy, gender equality policies, or the organisation of care itself.
